explanation: In Ireland and Scotland, lanterns for the night were traditionally carved from turnips. Emigrants to North America found the local pumpkins bigger and easier to carve.

claims.text: Samhain, from which Halloween partly developed, was a festival of the Celts, in particular the Gaels of Ireland and Scotland.
Samhain was not a Roman, Viking or Saxon festival.
In Ireland and Scotland, lanterns for Halloween night were traditionally carved from turnips.
Irish and Scottish emigrants to North America took to pumpkins, which were bigger and easier to carve.

evidence.restatement: Samhain was the Gaelic (Celtic) festival of Ireland, Scotland and the Isle of Man that fed into Halloween.
Samhain was not a Roman, Norse or Anglo-Saxon festival.
In Ireland and Scotland, Halloween lanterns were traditionally carved from turnips and other root vegetables.
Irish and Scottish emigrants in North America took up pumpkins, which are larger and easier to hollow out and carve.
Samhain, at the start of November, marked the end of the harvest and the beginning of winter, the dark half of the year.
